USMLE-style practice · Pharmacology

A new acid-base disturbance

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

A 28-year-old woman taking topiramate for epilepsy reports fatigue. Sodium is 140 mEq/L, chloride 113 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 17 mEq/L. Creatinine, lactate, and glucose are normal; urine ketones are negative. She has no diarrhea. Which mechanism best explains these findings?

  1. Accumulation of ketoacids from insulin deficiency
  2. Gastric hydrogen ion loss
  3. Primary alveolar hypoventilation
  4. Renal bicarbonate loss from carbonic anhydrase inhibition
  5. Accumulation of lactate from tissue hypoperfusion
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

Renal bicarbonate loss from carbonic anhydrase inhibition

The anion gap is 10. Topiramate can cause renal bicarbonate loss and hyperchloremic acidosis.

Understanding the options

Renal bicarbonate loss from carbonic anhydrase inhibition
The anion gap is 10. Topiramate can cause renal bicarbonate loss and hyperchloremic acidosis.
Accumulation of lactate from tissue hypoperfusion
Lactate is normal, and the anion gap is not increased.
Accumulation of ketoacids from insulin deficiency
Normal glucose and absent ketonuria argue against diabetic ketoacidosis.
Gastric hydrogen ion loss
Loss of gastric acid usually produces metabolic alkalosis.
Primary alveolar hypoventilation
This produces respiratory acidosis rather than a primary bicarbonate deficit.
